name: Permutation Separation
description: You are given a permutation $$$p_1, p_2, \dots , p_n$$$ (an array where each integer from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ appears exactly once). The weight of the $$$i$$$-th element of this permutation is $$$a_i$$$. At first, you separate your permutation into two non-empty sets — prefix and suffix. More formally, the first set contains elements $$$p_1, p_2, \dots , p_k$$$, the second — $$$p_{k+1}, p_{k+2}, \dots , p_n$$$, where $$$1 \le k \lt n$$$. After that, you may move elements between sets. The operation you are allowed to do is to choose some element of the first set and move it to the second set, or vice versa (move from the second set to the first). You have to pay $$$a_i$$$ dollars to move the element $$$p_i$$$. Your goal is to make it so that each element of the first set is less than each element of the second set. Note that if one of the sets is empty, this condition is met. For example, if $$$p = [3, 1, 2]$$$ and $$$a = [7, 1, 4]$$$, then the optimal strategy is: separate $$$p$$$ into two parts $$$[3, 1]$$$ and $$$[2]$$$ and then move the $$$2$$$-element into first set (it costs $$$4$$$). And if $$$p = [3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 4]$$$, $$$a = [9, 1, 9, 9, 1, 9]$$$, then the optimal strategy is: separate $$$p$$$ into two parts $$$[3, 5, 1]$$$ and $$$[6, 2, 4]$$$, and then move the $$$2$$$-element into first set (it costs $$$1$$$), and $$$5$$$-element into second set (it also costs $$$1$$$). Calculate the minimum number of dollars you have to spend.
input_specification: The first line contains one integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the length of permutation. The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$p_1, p_2, \dots , p_n$$$ ($$$1 \le p_i \le n$$$). It's guaranteed that this sequence contains each element from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$ exactly once. The third line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \dots , a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$).
output_specification: Print one integer — the minimum number of dollars you have to spend.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1295E — Permutation Separation [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
